interviewQuestions.question: Explain the kernel trick without the math — what's actually happening?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Picture red and blue dots scattered and tangled together on a flat table — no straight line anywhere on that table separates them cleanly. Now imagine lifting each dot upward according to some rule, say, higher the farther it sits from the center of the table: the reds, clustered near the center, stay low; the blues, scattered toward the edges, rise higher. Once lifted into this new, taller space, a flat sheet slid in at the right height now separates reds from blues perfectly — something no flat line on the original tabletop could ever do.

That lift is exactly what mapping data into a higher-dimensional space accomplishes: a boundary that's impossible to draw in the original, low-dimensional space becomes trivially easy (a flat line or plane) once the data is projected into more dimensions. The catch is that actually performing this lift explicitly — computing the new higher-dimensional coordinates for every single data point — can be computationally expensive, and for some useful mappings (the RBF kernel's implicit space, for instance) the target space is literally infinite-dimensional, meaning you couldn't write out the lifted coordinates even if you wanted to.

The kernel trick is the realization that SVM training never actually needs each point's literal lifted coordinates — it only ever needs to know how two lifted points relate to each other, specifically their dot product in that higher space. A kernel function is a shortcut that computes exactly that relationship directly from the two points' *original*, unlifted coordinates, without ever materializing the lift itself. So you get the mathematical benefit of the lift — a separating boundary that exists in the higher space — while paying only the computational cost of working in the original, low-dimensional space.

**Testing:** whether you can convey the geometric intuition (lift, then measure relationships without ever computing the lift) plainly, rather than reciting the dot-product definition without the picture behind it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The kernel trick, in plain language

interviewQuestions.question: Why does an SVM's decision boundary depend only on the support vectors, while a linear regression's fit depends on every single point? What's structurally different?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The difference comes directly from what each model's optimization objective actually penalizes. Linear regression minimizes squared error across every training point simultaneously — every point contributes a nonzero term to the loss (unless its residual is exactly zero, which essentially never happens with real data), so every point exerts some pull on where the fitted line ultimately lands, even points far from the line that are already well-predicted.

An SVM's objective is structured completely differently: it's explicitly trying to maximize the margin — the distance from the decision boundary to the nearest point of each class — and the optimization only cares about the points that are closest to that boundary, since those are the only ones actually constraining how wide the margin can be. A point sitting comfortably far from the boundary, deep in its own class's territory, contributes nothing to the margin-maximization objective and could be moved, or removed from the dataset entirely, without changing the SVM's solution at all — the mathematical formulation (specifically, in the dual optimization problem) assigns exactly zero weight to non-support-vector points.

This has a genuinely useful practical consequence: an SVM's solution is defined by a potentially small subset of the training data (the support vectors), which is part of why SVMs can generalize well even from limited data — the model isn't being pulled around by every point's individual noise, only by the handful of points that actually define the boundary's position. It also means an SVM can be surprisingly robust to adding more well-separated, non-borderline data, since those new points simply won't become support vectors and won't change the existing solution.

**Testing:** whether you can trace this back to the different optimization objectives (minimize error everywhere vs. maximize margin from the nearest points) rather than just stating the support-vector property as a fact to memorize.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why only support vectors matter

interviewQuestions.question: Your team wants to train a kernel SVM on a dataset with 5 million rows and is surprised training won't finish in a reasonable time. What's the actual bottleneck, and what would you recommend instead?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The bottleneck is a direct consequence of how kernel SVM training is computed, not a configuration issue a bigger machine fixes. Training requires computing the kernel function's value between every pair of training points, since the kernel implicitly represents pairwise relationships in the (possibly infinite-dimensional) transformed space the optimization is defined over. That pairwise computation scales roughly quadratically to cubically with row count depending on the solver — at 5 million rows, that's on the order of trillions of pairwise kernel evaluations, before even accounting for the optimization iterations needed. This is a fundamentally different scaling behavior from a linear model, whose training cost scales roughly linearly with rows, which is exactly why linear models remain tractable at this scale while kernel methods become impractical well before reaching millions of rows.

This scaling wall is the actual, well-documented reason SVMs largely faded from large-scale production use once datasets grew into the millions-of-rows range that's now routine — the field's data volumes grew past where kernel methods stay computationally tractable, not that the algorithm got worse.

My recommendation: at this scale, a kernel SVM isn't the right tool regardless of its theoretical properties. I'd reach for a linear SVM or logistic regression if a linear or near-linear boundary is adequate (both scale roughly linearly), or a gradient-boosted tree ensemble if the boundary is genuinely non-linear and complex — tree ensembles scale far better than kernel methods while still capturing non-linear decision boundaries, exactly the gap kernel SVMs used to fill before tree-based methods matured to cover it at production scale.

**Testing:** whether you understand the specific quadratic-to-cubic scaling mechanism behind the bottleneck, and can recommend concrete scale-appropriate alternatives rather than just saying "SVMs don't scale."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why kernel SVMs don't scale to millions of rows
